children: By Gregor Stuart Hunter
Asian stocks tumbled early on Wednesday as fresh US tariff threats hit sentiment and a tech-led rally fizzled, with the region's chip-heavy markets bearing the brunt of the selloff.
MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MISX00000PUS) was down 2.3%, led by a drop of as much as 5.3% in South Korean shares
and a 5.1% decline at the worst point in Taiwan
TWSE:TAIEX
Japan's Nikkei 225
fell as much as 2.9%, while S&P 500 e-mini futures
were 0.3% lower.
Risk appetite weakened after media reports the Trump administration was preparing to release findings of a trade investigation that could pave the way for new tariff measures.

The US Trade Representative's office is preparing to release the findings of the probe into alleged excess industrial capacity among 16 major US trading partners, including China and the EU, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters on Tuesday.

"The re-emergence of tariffs from the USTR has been met with a collective sigh from investors," said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone Group Ltd in Melbourne. "Much like the US debt ceiling, which is also making an unwelcome comeback onto the radar, traders appear reluctant to commit significant capital on the headlines alone."
Overnight, stocks on Wall Street were mixed, with the S&P 500
CBOE:SPX
down 0.5% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite
off 1.5%, while the small-cap Russell 2000
gained 0.6% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average
rallied 0.9%. Attention now turns to US core PCE data due on Wednesday ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday later in the week.
"Wall Street pared its Monday advance as sobriety returned to the market and a focus returned to fundamentals," said Kyle Rodda, senior market analyst at Capital.com in Melbourne.
The moves followed data showing US consumer confidence increased by more than expected in November, touching its highest level in nearly two years and better-than-expected earnings from Dell
on surging AI server demand. The shares rose 4.1% in after-hours trading.
Nvidia
surrendered some of its gains after Jensen Huang's return as CEO earlier this week, falling 5.9%, while Anthropic
fell 6.5% to below its IPO price.
Australian shares
slid 0.9% and the Australian dollar
strengthened 0.2% after the release of data showing consumer prices climbed by more than expected in October as fuel and clothing jumped.

The annualised trimmed mean measure of 3.8% means inflation is still running well above target and ramps up pressure on the Reserve Bank of Australia, which has already raised rates by 125 basis points this year.
In commodities, Brent crude
opened 0.5% lower at $90.97 in Asia after a choppy session on Tuesday, which saw crude prices settle more than 2% higher as new attacks were reported on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Copper
and tin
prices fell sharply on Tuesday, giving up all of the previous session's gains as the fizzling AI rally weighed on industrial metals, while aluminium
sank to a 13-month low.
